paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Electromagnetic induction happens when the magnetic field around a conductor, such as a wire, is changing. That change sets up an electromotive force, or emf, across the conductor. If the wire is joined to an electrical load, a current flows.

paragraphs.heading: Who found it
paragraphs.text: Michael Faraday is usually given the credit, and he published the discovery in 1831. Joseph Henry found the same effect on his own in 1832. James Clerk Maxwell later described it with mathematics, and the result became known as Faraday's law of induction.

paragraphs.heading: Faraday's iron ring
paragraphs.text: On August 29, 1831, Faraday wound two wires around opposite sides of an iron ring. He connected one wire to a galvanometer and watched it while he hooked the other wire up to a battery. It showed a short burst of current, which he called a "wave of electricity", at the moment of connection and another at the moment of disconnection. What mattered was the change in magnetic flux at those two moments.

paragraphs.heading: More ways to make a current
paragraphs.text: Within two months Faraday had found other forms of induction. Pushing a bar magnet quickly into and out of a coil of wire gave brief currents. Spinning a copper disk near the magnet, with a sliding contact, gave a steady direct current; this became known as Faraday's disk. He explained it all with an idea he called lines of force, which most scientists of his day rejected, mainly because it had no mathematics. Maxwell was the exception and built his quantitative theory on it.

paragraphs.heading: Flux and direction
paragraphs.text: Faraday's law is built on magnetic flux through the area enclosed by a loop of wire. You can picture flux as the number of magnetic field lines passing through the loop. In 1834 Heinrich Lenz stated a law that gives the direction of the induced emf and current. Faraday's law was later widened into the Maxwell–Faraday equation, which is one of Maxwell's four equations of electromagnetism.

paragraphs.heading: One law, two effects
paragraphs.text: Faraday's law covers two different effects. Motional emf comes from a magnetic force on a wire that is moving, while transformer emf comes from an electric force set up by a changing magnetic field. This is thought to be a unique case of one basic law explaining two such different things. Albert Einstein noticed that both cases are a conductor and a magnet moving relative to each other, and the outcome is the same whichever one moves. That idea was one of the main paths that led him to special relativity.

paragraphs.heading: Generators and their cost
paragraphs.text: Relative motion between a circuit and a magnetic field is what makes electrical generators work. Moving a magnet past a conductor, or the other way round, creates an emf, and with a load attached, the energy of motion becomes electrical energy. In Faraday's disk, the current turns the rim into an electromagnet that resists the spinning, which is an example of Lenz's law. The energy needed to keep the disk turning equals the electrical energy produced, plus losses such as friction and heating, and the same is true of all generators.

paragraphs.heading: Where it is used
paragraphs.text: Induction has many uses. Inductors and transformers depend on it, and so do electric motors and generators.
